analogy.p: The Mr is like the total weight of a shopping basket: you look up the weight of each item (Ar), multiply by how many of that item you have (the subscript), and add everything up. A bracket is like a bag containing several items: if you have 2 bags, you double everything in the bag, not just the first item. The analogy breaks down because the 'items' (atoms) are far too small to weigh, so we use relative values with no units, and real shopping weights are not averages of different versions of the same product the way an Ar is for isotopes.
analogy.t: A shopping basket at the till

bullets: **Ar = relative atomic mass**: the mass of an atom of an element compared with the mass of an atom of carbon-12 (which is defined as 12).
In the periodic table the **larger number** of the pair is the relative atomic mass; the **smaller number** is the atomic number (number of protons). For sodium, Ar = 23 and atomic number = 11.
Ar has **no units** because it is a ratio, so you never write 'g' after an Ar value.
Common values to recognise: H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Mg = 24, Al = 27, S = 32, Cl = 35.5, K = 39, Ca = 40, Fe = 56, Cu = 63.5, Zn = 65.
Always use the Ar value given in the question or data, even if it differs slightly from your memory (for example Cu = 63.5, not 64).
Link: Ar is the starting point for every quantitative calculation in the topic (moles, reacting masses, percentage yield, atom economy).
core.p: Every atom has a tiny mass, far too small to use in grams, so chemists compare atoms using **relative atomic mass, Ar**. This is a scale on which the carbon-12 atom is given a mass of exactly 12, and every other atom is compared with it. Because it is a comparison, it has **no units**. The Ar of each element is given in the periodic table, and in the exam you are given a periodic table (or a list of Ar values) so you never need to memorise them. The key skill is picking out the correct number from the table.

bullets: **Isotopes** have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons.
Ar = (isotope mass 1 × % abundance 1 + isotope mass 2 × % abundance 2) ÷ 100.
The Ar is closer to the mass of the more abundant isotope, which is a quick way to check your answer is sensible.
Copper is 63.5 for the same reason: it is a mixture of copper-63 and copper-65.
Elements with only one natural isotope (for example fluorine, Ar = 19) have a whole-number Ar.
Link: isotopes are covered in atomic structure; the same weighted-average idea appears in that topic.
core.h: Why some Ar values are not whole numbers
core.p: Most elements exist as a mixture of **isotopes**, which are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, so they have different masses. The Ar printed in the table is a **weighted mean (average) mass that takes account of the abundance of each isotope**. This is why chlorine has an Ar of 35.5: it is a mixture of about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37. No individual chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5; the figure is an average. Figure 5 shows this calculation.

bullets: **Mr = sum of the Ar values of all the atoms shown in the formula.**
Mr has **no units**. The Mr of water is 18, not 18 g. (The molar mass is 18 g/mol, which is a different idea covered under moles.)
The word 'formula' is used because many compounds, such as sodium chloride, are giant ionic lattices with no separate molecules. The formula (NaCl) shows the simplest ratio of ions.
For a diatomic element the formula has two atoms, so Mr(O2) = 2 × 16 = 32, Mr(H2) = 2 × 1 = 2, Mr(Cl2) = 2 × 35.5 = 71 and Mr(N2) = 2 × 14 = 28.
For an element written as a single atom, such as Mg or Fe, Mr is the same as Ar.
Link: the same value is the mass in grams of one mole of the substance.
core.p: The **relative formula mass, Mr**, of a compound is the **sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula**. This is the exact wording the specification uses, and it is worth learning. A formula tells you how many atoms of each element are present, so you add up the Ar of every atom that appears in it. Like Ar, Mr is a relative value, so it has **no units**. For simple molecules it is often called relative molecular mass, but the method is identical.

bullets: **Step 1:** write the correct formula (for example H2SO4).
**Step 2:** list each element and count its atoms from the small subscript numbers after the symbol: H = 2, S = 1, O = 4.
**Step 3:** find each Ar from the periodic table: H = 1, S = 32, O = 16.
**Step 4:** multiply atoms by Ar: 2 × 1 = 2; 1 × 32 = 32; 4 × 16 = 64.
If no subscript is written the number of atoms is **1**.
Show the working in a line like 'Mr = (2 × 1) + 32 + (4 × 16) = 98' so method marks are available.
Do not write units for Mr; do not round Ar values that are given to one decimal place such as 35.5.
core.h: Method: calculating Mr step by step
core.p: A reliable method earns the marks even if you slip on arithmetic. Write the formula, list each element, count the atoms, multiply by Ar, then add. Marks in the exam are usually given for correct Ar values, correct multiplication and the correct total, so showing each stage protects you. Figure 1 shows the layout for sulfuric acid, H2SO4.

bullets: **Mg(NO3)2** contains 1 Mg, 2 N and 6 O (because 3 × 2 = 6), so Mr = 24 + 28 + 96 = **148**.
A useful check is to work out the group first: OH = 16 + 1 = 17, then Ca(OH)2 = 40 + 2 × 17 = 74.
Count each atom on a rough list before multiplying so you do not miss one.
Link: bracketed formulas are the ionic compounds containing compound ions (hydroxide, nitrate, sulfate), which you meet in chemical changes.
core.p: When a formula contains brackets, the small number written **outside** the bracket multiplies **every atom inside** the bracket. Students lose marks by multiplying only the first atom, or by forgetting that the subscript outside applies to atoms with their own subscript too. Treat the bracket as a group: work out the Mr of the group, then multiply the group by the number outside. Figure 2 shows Ca(OH)2.

bullets: Water H2O = 18; carbon dioxide CO2 = 44; ammonia NH3 = 17; methane CH4 = 16.
Hydrogen chloride HCl = 36.5; sodium chloride NaCl = 58.5; sodium hydroxide NaOH = 40; potassium hydroxide KOH = 56.
Sulfuric acid H2SO4 = 98; nitric acid HNO3 = 63; sodium carbonate Na2CO3 = 106.
Calcium carbonate CaCO3 = 100; calcium oxide CaO = 56; magnesium oxide MgO = 40; magnesium chloride MgCl2 = 95.
Aluminium oxide Al2O3 = 102; iron(III) oxide Fe2O3 = 160; copper(II) oxide CuO = 79.5; copper(II) sulfate CuSO4 = 159.5.
Glucose C6H12O6 = 180; ethanol C2H5OH = 46.
Link: 100 for CaCO3 makes percentage and mole calculations easy, so it is a favourite exam example.
core.p: With practice you will quickly recognise the Mr of the compounds that appear again and again in exam questions. Knowing them lets you check your answers fast and makes mole calculations quicker. You do not have to memorise them, because you can always calculate them from the Ar values, but familiarity helps you spot arithmetic errors.

bullets: **Simple molecular substance** (H2O, CO2, CH4): the formula shows the atoms in one molecule.
**Giant ionic lattice** (NaCl, MgO, CaCl2): the formula shows the simplest ratio of ions, called a **formula unit**.
**Giant covalent structure** (SiO2, diamond): the formula shows the ratio of atoms in the structure.
The method (add up the Ar values in the formula) is the same in every case.
Ions are treated as atoms for this purpose because the mass of the electrons gained or lost is negligible.
Link: the structure and bonding topic explains why ionic compounds have formula units rather than molecules.
core.h: Ionic compounds and molecules: same method, different words
core.p: The specification uses the term relative formula mass for any substance, but you may see **relative molecular mass** used for simple covalent molecules. The calculation is exactly the same. The important idea is why the word 'formula' is used: an ionic compound such as sodium chloride is not made of separate molecules, it is a giant lattice of ions, so you can only say that its formula, NaCl, shows the ratio of ions. The Mr is therefore the mass of one formula unit.

bullets: The balancing numbers in front of formulas multiply the Mr of the **whole** formula: in 2MgO the Mr total is 2 × 40 = 80.
**2Mg + O2 → 2MgO**: reactants 2 × 24 + 32 = 80; products 2 × (24 + 16) = 80. They match.
**CaCO3 → CaO + CO2**: 100 on the left; 56 + 44 = 100 on the right.
If the totals do not match, either the equation is not balanced or a formula or Ar value is wrong. This is a strong self-check.
The totals are in the same units as the masses in the reaction, so 80 units of reactants give 80 units of products. This gives reacting masses (for example 48 g Mg gives 80 g MgO).
Link: reacting-mass calculations are built directly on this idea.
core.h: Mr in balanced equations and conservation of mass
core.p: The sum of the relative formula masses of the reactants in the quantities shown in a balanced equation **equals** the sum of the relative formula masses of the products. This is the law of conservation of mass written in numbers: atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass stays the same. The big numbers in front of formulas multiply the whole formula. You can use this as a check that an equation is balanced and correctly written, as shown in Figure 3.

bullets: **% by mass of an element = (Ar × number of atoms of that element) ÷ Mr of the compound × 100.**
Ammonium nitrate NH4NO3: Mr = 28 + 4 + 48 = 80, so % N = 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = **35%**.
Calcium carbonate CaCO3: % Ca = 40 ÷ 100 × 100 = **40%**; % C = 12%; % O = 48%.
Count **all** the atoms of the element in the formula, not just one, which is where marks are lost.
The percentages for all elements should add up to 100% (allowing for rounding).
Link: used to compare fertilisers and to compare ores when extracting metals.
core.h: Percentage by mass of an element in a compound
core.p: The relative formula mass lets you find what fraction of a compound's mass is made by one element. The formula is the Ar of the element multiplied by the number of its atoms in the formula, divided by Mr of the compound, then multiplied by 100. This is a common calculation and it is also a good place to check your work: all the percentages of the elements in a compound must add up to 100%. Figure 4 shows ammonium nitrate, a nitrogen fertiliser.

bullets: Compound XO has Mr = 40: Ar of X = 40 − 16 = 24, so X is **magnesium**.
Compound XCl2 has Mr = 111: 111 − (2 × 35.5) = 111 − 71 = 40, so X is **calcium**.
Compound X2O has Mr = 62: 62 − 16 = 46; 46 ÷ 2 = 23, so X is **sodium** (Na2O).
Always divide by the number of atoms of the unknown if there is more than one.
Check by adding the Ar values back together to see if you get the original Mr.
Link: used in identifying metals from the mass of their oxide, chloride or sulfate.
core.h: Working backwards: finding an unknown Ar or element
core.p: Sometimes you are given the Mr and asked to identify an unknown. Subtract the Ar values you do know from the Mr, then divide by the number of atoms of the unknown. Then use the periodic table to find which element has that Ar. This reverses the normal method and tests whether you understand that Mr is a sum.

bullets: Write the correct formula first. Remember the charges: magnesium oxide is MgO, sodium oxide is Na2O, aluminium oxide is Al2O3.
Use a table (element, number of atoms, Ar, total) for long formulas, as in Figure 2.
Do not confuse **atomic number** (smaller number) with Ar (larger number) when reading the periodic table.
Give the answer with no units for Mr; if you give the mass of a mole, use g/mol or g.
Use the Ar values from the question (35.5 for chlorine, 63.5 for copper) and do not round them unless told to.
Check your answer is sensible: Mr should be bigger than the Ar of any single atom in the formula.
Link: these habits carry forward to moles, concentration and yield.
core.h: Presenting calculations and avoiding common slips
core.p: Calculation marks depend on method as well as the answer. Setting out your working clearly lets the examiner give method marks even if the arithmetic is wrong, and it makes it easier for you to spot an error. For Mr questions, write every atom and its Ar, then show the total. Check the formula you are using is correct first, since an incorrect formula (for example MgO2) wastes the whole calculation.

bullets: **Moles:** moles = mass ÷ Mr, so a correct Mr is essential.
**Reacting masses:** compare Mr totals from the equation to scale masses up or down.
**Atom economy (triple):** atom economy = Mr of desired product ÷ sum of Mr of all products × 100.
**Percentage yield (triple):** uses the theoretical mass worked out from the equation and Mr values.
**Empirical formula:** divide masses by Ar to get moles, then find the simplest whole-number ratio.
**Concentration:** converting g/dm3 to mol/dm3 needs Mr.
**Mass spectrometry (chemical analysis):** the molecular ion peak gives the Mr of the compound.
core.p: Relative formula mass is a gateway skill. Almost every quantitative question in GCSE chemistry starts by finding an Mr. You use it directly to work out moles (mass ÷ Mr), reacting masses, percentage yield and atom economy, and you also use it with concentrations and gas volumes. In chemical analysis and organic chemistry you will meet Mr again, for example in mass spectrometry.

exam: **Command words:** 'Calculate' needs working and a final answer, usually with units only if the answer is a mass or amount (Mr has none). 'Show that' needs every step and a final value that matches the given figure.
**State what Mr means (1 mark):** 'the sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula'. Learn this wording.
**1 mark:** a correct Ar from the table or a correct single Mr. **2 marks:** correct method plus correct answer, often with one mark for counting the atoms correctly.
**3 marks:** three stages such as formula, Ar values and total, or an Mr followed by a percentage by mass. Show every line.
**Explain why the Ar of chlorine is 35.5 (2-3 marks):** chlorine has two isotopes (Cl-35 and Cl-37); Ar is the average mass taking into account the abundance of each isotope.
**Conservation of mass check (2 marks):** calculate the total Mr of reactants and products and state they are equal, so mass is conserved.
**Percentage mass (3 marks):** (Ar × number of atoms) ÷ Mr × 100; check that all elements add to 100%.
**Unknown element (3 marks):** subtract known Ar values from Mr, divide by the number of atoms, then name the element.
**Layout:** write the formula, then the atoms and Ar values, then the sum. Examiners award method marks only if they can see it.
**Check:** is Mr bigger than the largest single Ar in the formula? Did you use brackets properly? Did you use the Ar given (Cl = 35.5)?

mistakes.r: Mr and Ar are relative values with no units.
mistakes.w: Writing units such as 'g' after Mr or Ar.

mistakes.r: Use the larger number, the relative atomic mass.
mistakes.w: Using the atomic number (smaller number) as the Ar.

mistakes.r: The number outside the bracket multiplies every atom inside it: 40 + 2 × 16 + 2 × 1 = 74.
mistakes.w: Ignoring the number outside a bracket, e.g. Ca(OH)2 = 40 + 16 + 1.

mistakes.r: Multiply the whole Mr by the balancing number: 2 × 40 = 80.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the balancing number when finding the total Mr in an equation, e.g. using 40 for 2MgO.

mistakes.r: Use the values given: Cl = 35.5, Cu = 63.5.
mistakes.w: Rounding chlorine to 35 or copper to 64.

mistakes.r: It is a weighted mean that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes (about 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37).
mistakes.w: Saying the Ar of chlorine is 35.5 because an atom weighs 35.5.

mistakes.r: Count all atoms of that element: 2 × 14 = 28, so % N = 28 ÷ 80 × 100 = 35%.
mistakes.w: Counting only one atom of an element when finding % by mass, e.g. N in NH4NO3 as 14.

mistakes.r: Use the full formula: SO4 means 1 S and 4 O.
mistakes.w: Adding up Ar of elements listed in the name only (e.g. missing the oxygen in a sulfate).

summary: You must be able to use relative atomic masses (Ar) from the periodic table to calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of a substance, including those with brackets, and use it to show that mass is conserved in a balanced equation and to calculate percentage by mass. It matters because Mr is the first step in every quantitative calculation in chemistry.

terms.d: The average mass of the atoms of an element, taking account of the abundance of its isotopes, compared with carbon-12 (given a value of 12). It has no units.
The sum of the relative atomic masses (Ar) of the atoms in the numbers shown in the formula. It has no units.
The Mr of a simple covalent molecule; it is found in the same way as relative formula mass.
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom; the smaller number for each element in the periodic table.
Shows the types of atoms (or ions) and the number of each in the simplest unit of a substance.
The small number written after a symbol in a formula showing how many atoms of that element there are.
The simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound, such as NaCl.
A molecule made of two atoms, such as H2, N2, O2, F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2.
An equation with the same number of each type of atom on both sides, showing the conservation of mass.
No atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
The mass of an element in a compound as a percentage of the mass of the whole compound.
An average that takes account of how much of each value there is, used for Ar with isotopes.
A group of atoms with an overall charge, such as OH−, NO3− and SO42−; written in brackets when more than one is present.
